newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Socialists pick candidates, a year early.
newsitem.headline: French Socialists pick candidates, a year early.

text.p: French Socialists on Saturday endorsed a host of new faces to be their candidates in the next general elections and left the door open to an electoral pact with the Communist Party.
Some 600 delegates of France's largest opposition party approved a list of candidates, close to 30 percent of whom are women, for elections due by early next year.

"From the day after this conference, all our candidates will be able to be on the ground, less than a year before the elections, to prepare our future campaign and multiply our strengths," Socialist leader Lionel Jospin said in a speech.
Over the next few days, he added, eight million copies will be printed of a manifesto-like outline of economic and welfare proposals.

The Socialists will enter the election with a strongly-refurbished slate. According to a party official, 48 percent of the candidates picked for the next poll did not run for office in the 1993 elections.
Jospin himself will stand for parliament in the Haute-Garonne department in southwestern France, where he lost his seat in 1993.

Jospin said progress had been made on electoral pacts with the Greens and the small Radical Socialist Party, but that talks were still under way with the Communists who are reluctant to drop their hostility to plans for a single European currency.

Socialist spokesman Francois Hollande told reporters that there were still "good chances" of an electoral pact with the Citizens' Movement led by former Defence Minister and former Socialist Jean-Pierre Chevenement.
Jospin appealed to other leftist forces last month to forge a pact "to govern together". But he insisted his party would not give up the single currency.
But differences surfaced within the traditionally-fractious Socialist Party itself.

Jean-Luc Melenchon, a senator from a leftist Socialist faction, said a local election due in Vitrolles in southern France on Sunday, which the far-right National Front is poised to win, should sound alarm bells.
He called for tighter accords with the Communists than Jospin has so far envisaged, possibly through a common platform.
"(Vitrolles) is why we need a government pact. We need a proper accord with the Communist Party...We should govern with the Communists," he said.
